rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Evolution is inferred, not assumed. Morphology shows homologous organs — the same bones serving different lives in human, whale, bat and horse — proving divergent evolution from common ancestry; analogous wings of butterfly and bird show convergence instead; vestigial appendix and coccyx are inherited footnotes; *Archaeopteryx* bridges reptile and bird.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Homologous: same structure, different function, common origin (divergent evolution)
Analogous: different structure, same function, different origin (convergent evolution)
Vestigial: reduced remnant of an ancestral organ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Homologous vs analogous:** homologous = same bones, different jobs (divergence); analogous = different parts, same job (convergence). Memory: "Homo = same anatomy; Analog = same action."  ·  **Vestigial vs atavistic:** vestigial = permanently reduced remnant (appendix); atavistic = rare reappearance of an ancestral trait (human tail).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB frequently asks for homologous vs analogous organs with examples.  ·  Vestigial organs in humans (appendix, coccyx) are a common short-answer.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Archaeopteryx*** — Jurassic fossil with feathers AND teeth, clawed wings, bony tail: the reptile–bird link.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Asked in 2021, 2022 and 2024 — the most repeated evolution topic. Master the homologous/analogous distinction cold.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Differentiate homologous vs analogous  ·  List 3 vestigial organs

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Same bones, new jobs = homologous; new bones, same job = analogous."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Q.** What are vestigial organs? **Answer.** Reduced, functionless remnants of organs that were **useful in ancestors** — e.g. the human appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth and nictitating membrane, and the whale's pelvic bones.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: homologous vs analogous (2021, 2024), evidences with morphological + paleontological examples (2022, 2024).

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: 2.1 Morphological and anatomical evidences (NEB 2021, 2022, 2024) · Evidence | Definition | Example | What it shows · **Homologous organs** | Same basic structure and origin, **different functions** | Forelimbs of human (grasping), whale (swimming), bat (flying), horse (running) — same bones: humerus, radius-ulna, carpals, digits | **Divergent evolution** from a common ancestor · **Analogous organs** | Different structures and origins, **same function** |…  ·  2.2 Paleontological evidence (NEB 2022, 2024) · Aspect | Detail · Fossil | Any preserved remains or traces of past life (bones, shells, impressions, footprints, amber, petrification) · Dating | **Relative** (stratigraphy — deeper is older); **absolute** (radioactive dating — C-14 for <50,000 yr; U-Pb, K-Ar for older rocks) · Sequence | Simple prokaryotes (3.5 bya) → eukaryotes → invertebrates → fish → amphibians → reptiles → birds/mammals → humans:…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Convergent vs divergent evolution:** homologous structures diverge from one ancestor; analogous structures converge from different ancestors — the same two words explain both sides of the comparison question.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Morphological: homologous (forelimb of human/whale/bat/horse — divergent, common ancestry), analogous (butterfly vs bird wing — convergent), vestigial (appendix, coccyx), connecting links (Archaeopteryx, Peripatus).  ·  Paleontological: fossils dated by stratigraphy and radioisotopes; sequence simple→complex; transitional fossils (Archaeopteryx, Tiktaalik).  ·  Embryological: shared early embryos (gill pouches, tail). Biochemical: same genetic code; cytochrome c similarity tracks relatedness. Biogeographical: marsupials of Australia, Galápagos finches.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Human and chimpanzee genomes are about 98–99% identical — molecular evidence agreeing with anatomy.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Case for Evolution Evolution is not believed on authority; it is inferred from evidence — anatomical, fossil, embryological and biochemical. Each line of evidence is an independent witness, and they all agree: life shares common ancestry and has changed through time. NEB has asked this topic three years running (2021, 2022, 2024).  ·  ## 2.
